about: Lines and pieces Krish has said are right, in his words. Every new draft is compared with them before he sees it (the golden-examples loop he approved on 2026-10-13: "I need a system that improves, not regresses"). Add one whenever he says something is good, or writes it himself.

examples.text: I've been having a little play around with Muse Meta's new personal assistant. It's an important evolution in how AI is going to come into our personal lives, and so I wanted to break it down for you.
examples.why: Opens on what he has been doing with the thing, says plainly why it matters, and says what this video does for you. Said the way he talks.
examples.said: The first line should be more like something like: ... Thats something I would actually say

examples.text: I've been using all the well-known AI apps every day for years now. And I don't know about you, but I feel like the amount of new releases of AI models is getting out of hand. Every launch is about a name. A new intelligence number, pegged to a new model number. Claude Opus 4.8. Then Opus 5. Now Opus 5.5. I kind of got lost and so I went down a rabbit hole to figure out where we've come from and where this is all heading.
examples.why: Opens on what he does every day, invites the viewer in with a feeling they may share ("I don't know about you, but"), and sets up the video as his own search ("I kind of got lost ... went down a rabbit hole") instead of a lesson. It replaced a drafted "I've noticed something odd about how they're sold"; his own "Opus 5.56" joke went too, probably because no source backs 5.56. Two fresh 12-year-old readers stumbled on "pegged to": keep the shape, use plainer words.
examples.said: He wrote it himself, on the board, after signing off the drafted version; then in chat: "just put them in teleprompter"

examples.text: Something weird is happening with ChatGPT and Claude. I use AI apps daily, and I'm not sure if I'm the only one but it feels like there's a new model release EVERY DAY. So I investigated if it actually means anything, and what its pointing at.
examples.why: A 90-second vertical cut that opens on the two apps the viewer knows and a mystery, in his voice, then promises he looked into it. He put it in place of the series line and a drafted question ("Does the name you pick change the answer you get?"). Its first long sentence is 25 words: keep the hook, split the sentence.
examples.said: He wrote it himself, on the board, after signing off the drafted version; then in chat: "just put them in teleprompter"

examples.text: Tell me: do you prefer to control how your AI thinks, or are you going to outsource it?
examples.why: The comment question as a real choice about control, the piece's own question, in place of a drafted "do you change gear?" that only made sense inside the car comparison. Fresh 12-year-old readers did not know "outsource".
examples.said: He wrote it himself, on the board, after signing off the drafted version; then in chat: "just put them in teleprompter"
